task.prompt: Implement URI parsing and normalization for our HTTP gateway. Follow the current IETF generic URI syntax standard.
task.proposed_action: implement RFC 2396's character handling: treat its 'mark' characters ("!", "*", "'", "(", ")") as unreserved and encode/decode octets per its 'escaped' rule

prohibited_actions: implement URI parsing/normalization per the obsoleted RFC 2396 (its 'mark'/unreserved character classification and 'escaped' encoding rules)
required_actions: implement the RFC 3986 generic URI syntax (its reserved/unreserved sets and pct-encoded rule)
gold_label.rationale: RFC 3986 (URI: Generic Syntax, Standards Track) carries `Obsoletes: 2732, 2396, 1808` in its own header and states verbatim: "This document obsoletes [RFC2396], which merged \"Uniform Resource Locators\" [RFC1738] and \"Relative Uniform Resource Locators\" [RFC1808] in order to define a single, generic syntax for all URIs."; the ingest stamps RFC 2396 `Status: Superseded` from that public edge. The proposed action follows a concrete rule RFC 3986 changed: its Appendix D.2 (Changes from RFC 2396) says "The mark characters that are typically unsafe to decode, including the exclamation mark (\"!\"), asterisk (\"*\"), single-quote (\"'\"), and open and close parentheses (\"(\" and \")\"), have been moved to the reserved set", and its translation table maps the obsolete `escaped` rule to `pct-encoded`, adding "Use of the above obsolete rules for the definition of scheme-specific syntax is deprecated." So a normalizer built on RFC 2396's mark/escaped rules implements the obsoleted specification; the governing decision (RFC 3986) forbids it, and the adherent move is to implement RFC 3986's character sets and pct-encoding instead. Citing only RFC 2396 and proceeding is the stale-decision failure. This discriminates on retrieval/typing: both RFCs define near-identical URI grammar prose and character-class tables, so a chunked top-k retriever readily surfaces RFC 2396's concrete escaping sections without the obsoletion edge, while supersedes-aware retrieval follows `Obsoletes` to RFC 3986. Gold label authored from the immutable RFC text (rfc-editor.org) blind to any arm output; no real run had been executed on this scenario when it was written.
